title: It always passes the second time
note: Fictional unit. Your machine’s instructions for use, your unit’s written procedure, and the supervising nurse come first.
intro: It is Wednesday, 05:45. You are preparing machine HD-07 for Mrs. Carmen Reyes, who is due at 06:15. The machine fails its required pre-use pressure self-test, and the display names the test. Your coworker, Mr. Ronnie Castillo, says: “Restart it. That one always passes the second time.” Machine HD-09 is a spare.

n1.prompt: What do you do with HD-07?

choices.text: Write down the machine number and the exact message, label it out of use, and report to the nurse and the biomedical contact.
choices.feedback: A failed required test means the machine has not shown it is safe. The self-test checks the alarms that protect the patient. A test that fails sometimes is telling you that something is marginal.

choices.text: Restart it, and use it if it passes this time.
choices.feedback: Passing on a retry does not explain the failure. An unreliable alarm is worse than none, because people trust it. A machine that fails a required check stays out of service until an authorized person clears it.
choices.then: The nurse overhears and asks you to hold HD-07 and report it.

choices.text: Clear the message and carry on setting up; the biomedical team can look at it later.
choices.feedback: Clearing the message hides the evidence. It does not make the machine ready.
choices.then: You stop, record the message, label HD-07 out of use, and report it.

n2.scene: The nurse assigns spare machine HD-09 to Mrs. Reyes. It was used on Monday. Mr. Castillo says it is fine because it ran all of Monday without a problem.

choices.text: All of them: its identity, disinfection record and residual check, concentrates against the prescription, stabilization, and its own self-test.
choices.feedback: A substitute machine needs its own full set of checks. Monday’s run tells you nothing about today. The nurse can rearrange the schedule; nobody can undo a treatment started on an unsafe machine.

choices.text: Just its self-test, since it worked on Monday.
choices.feedback: A successful self-test confirms only what that test covers. It does not check the disinfection record, the residual disinfectant, or that the concentrates match the order.

choices.text: None. Set it up quickly so the patient is not late.
choices.feedback: Time pressure is real, but skipping checks is how a patient ends up on a machine with disinfectant inside or the wrong dialysate.

n3.scene: HD-09’s screen shows “ready,” but its log has no record that the disinfection after Monday’s last treatment ran, and no residual test is written.

choices.text: Do not use it yet. Tell the nurse; by procedure the machine is rinsed and tested for residual disinfectant, or disinfected again.
choices.feedback: You cannot tell whether it was disinfected or whether chemical remains inside. Disinfectant reaching a patient’s blood, and a machine that was never disinfected, are both serious harms.
choices.then: The nurse has it disinfected and rinsed. The residual disinfectant test is negative, and you write the actual result.

choices.text: The screen says ready, so the disinfection must have run.
choices.feedback: “Ready” tells you the machine passed its own start-up. It is not a record that disinfection ran or that the residual test was done. Never write “passed” for a check nobody did.
choices.then: The nurse checks the log, finds it blank, and has the machine disinfected and rinsed. The residual test is negative.

choices.text: Do a residual disinfectant test now; if it is negative, use it.
choices.feedback: A negative residual test is reassuring about chemical, but it does not show the machine was disinfected. Report the blank log; the procedure decides whether a rinse and test is enough or disinfection is repeated.
choices.then: The nurse decides to disinfect it again. The residual test afterward is negative.

n4.scene: Reading the labels against Mrs. Reyes’s prescription, you see that the acid concentrate jug at the station says potassium 2.0. Her prescription says potassium 3.0. The cap is the same color as the one she usually uses.

choices.text: Stop, tell the nurse, and connect the concentrate whose label matches the prescription; then let it stabilize before setup continues.
choices.feedback: The label, read against the prescription, is the only reliable check. The wrong potassium bath changes how much potassium leaves her blood, and the prescription is the physician’s decision.

choices.text: Use it. The cap color matches, and 2.0 and 3.0 are close.
choices.feedback: Never guess from the color of a container or cap. A different potassium bath is a different prescription, and only the physician can change it.
choices.then: The nurse stops you and swaps in the correct concentrate.

choices.text: Ask Mrs. Reyes which one she usually gets.
choices.feedback: The patient may not know, and her answer is not the order. Check the written prescription and tell the nurse.
choices.then: You check the prescription and tell the nurse, who swaps in the correct concentrate.

n5.scene: The nurse connected Mrs. Reyes at 06:30. At 08:10 the venous pressure has been climbing, the machine alarms, and you see dark streaks in the dialyzer and a clot forming in the venous chamber.

choices.text: Call the nurse now and tell her the pressure trend and what you see; have saline and a new circuit ready if she asks. Do not reset the alarm.
choices.feedback: Dark streaks, a clot in a chamber, and rising pressure mean the circuit is clotting. The nurse decides what to do; your job is to report what you see and have the supplies ready.

choices.text: Reset the alarm so the pump keeps running until the nurse finishes her round.
choices.feedback: Do not reset alarms to keep the pump going. A clotting circuit can block, and blood in a clotted circuit is not returned. Never silence an alarm before you know why it sounded.

choices.text: Write the pressure in the log and mention it to the nurse on her next round.
choices.feedback: Recording is right, but a clotting circuit cannot wait for the next round. Call the nurse now.

end.title: End of the shift
end.text: The nurse ends the clotted circuit and decides on the rest of the treatment with the physician. In the machine logs you write the exact HD-07 message and the hold, HD-09’s disinfection and residual results, the concentrate check, and the time of the clotting alarm. The biomedical team finds a failing pressure sensor in HD-07 and releases it two days later.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • A failed self-test means hold, record, report. Never restart it “to see if it passes this time.”
  • A replacement machine gets its own full checks.
  • “Ready” is not a disinfection record. A blank log means rinse and test, or disinfect again, by procedure.
  • Read labels against the prescription, never colors.
  • Never reset an alarm to keep the pump going. Call the nurse and report what you see.

See Operating the machine and Hold, escalate and document.
